title: Schwarzschild geometry and black holes
one_line_summary: Uses the conserved energy and angular momentum of Schwarzschild geodesics to build effective potentials and classify orbits (ISCO at 6M, photon orbit at 3M, perihelion advance, light bending by 4M/b, lensing). It then shows that r = 2M is only a coordinate singularity but is a one-way null horizon, using infall times and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates. From there it generalizes to event horizons and the black-hole theorems, explores the Kerr solution (frame dragging, ergosphere, horizon area, Penrose process), surveys the black holes seen in astronomy, and closes with a heuristic uncertainty-principle derivation of Hawking radiation and black-hole thermodynamics.
role_in_book: Chapter 10 derived the Schwarzschild exterior of a static star. This chapter takes that metric and applies the whole toolkit built so far: conserved momenta from symmetries (ch7), the weak-field limit and far-field mass and spin (ch8), curvature and geodesic deviation (ch6), and spacetime diagrams (ch1). It is the book's strong-field centerpiece. It delivers the classical solar-system tests (perihelion shift, light deflection), connects to the binary pulsar met in ch9, and builds the black-hole physics (horizons, Kerr, no-hair, area theorem) that ch12 needs for gravitational waves from black-hole mergers and ringdown. It also prepares ch13 by introducing dark matter from lensing and the naked Big Bang singularity. Like other late chapters it moves from derivation into a long observational survey with 2021-era numbers.

assumed_background.topic: Conserved covariant momentum components p_0 and p_phi when the metric is independent of t or phi
Schwarzschild line element in areal coordinates, its derivation, and the maximum mass of neutron stars
Four-momentum normalization p.p = -m^2, index raising with g^{alpha beta}, and energy measured by an observer as -p.U
Weak-field metric of a Newtonian source (Eq. 8.50) and defining M and J from the far field
Riemann tensor components, Christoffel symbols of diagonal metrics, and the geodesic deviation equation
Invariant hyperbolae and orthogonality of radial lines to them in special-relativistic spacetime diagrams
Gravitational redshift and the transverse Doppler effect
Geometrized units with G = c = 1 and masses expressed in km
Newtonian orbits: escape velocity, centrifugal effective potential, Kepler ellipses and Kepler's third law
Separable first-order ODEs, Taylor expansion to first order, completing the square, hyperbolic functions
Inverting a 2x2 symmetric matrix block and determinants
Black-body radiation, Stefan-Boltzmann law, first and second laws of thermodynamics, entropy
Energy-time uncertainty relation and the idea of vacuum fluctuations
Astronomical units and objects: arcseconds, parsecs, solar mass, X-ray binaries, quasars, galaxy clusters

learning_objectives: Reader can derive the conserved specific energy and angular momentum of Schwarzschild geodesics and reduce the motion to a one-dimensional radial energy equation for both massive particles and photons.
Reader can sketch the effective potentials for particles and photons and read off turning points, scattering, bound, circular (stable and unstable) and plunging orbits from an energy line.
Reader can derive the radii of circular orbits, show that stable circular orbits require J^2 > 12M^2, and obtain the ISCO at r = 6M and the unstable photon orbit at r = 3M.
Reader can compute the coordinate-time period of a circular orbit and explain why it coincides with Kepler's law and is what a distant observer measures.

Reader can perturb the orbit equation in u = 1/r about a circular orbit to obtain the perihelion advance 6 pi M^2/J^2 ~ 6 pi M/r and evaluate it for Mercury (43 arcsec per century) and for binary pulsars.
Reader can explain the post-Newtonian idea, relate Schwarzschild to isotropic coordinates at large r, and argue that Newtonian dynamics of slow bodies is controlled by g_00 alone.
Reader can derive the light-deflection angle 4M/b, evaluate 1.74 arcsec at the solar limb, and explain physically why the Newtonian corpuscular value is half as large.
Reader can describe gravitational lensing phenomena (multiple images, arcs, magnification, microlensing) and what they reveal about dark matter.
Reader can show that a radially infalling particle reaches r = 2M in finite proper time but infinite Schwarzschild coordinate time, and interpret this as a coordinate singularity.
Reader can explain why r becomes timelike inside r = 2M and why everything inside must reach r = 0, making r = 2M a horizon.

Reader can write down Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates, state the metric in them, and read a Kruskal diagram: 45-degree light cones, hyperbolae of constant r, lines of constant t, horizon, singularity, and which regions are physical for a collapsing star.
Reader can state the global definition of an event horizon, explain why it is teleological, and distinguish it from a locally trapped surface.
Reader can summarize the key black-hole theorems and conjectures: uniqueness (Kerr), area theorem, singularity theorems, cosmic censorship, and linear stability results.
Reader can work with the Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates to find the frame-dragging angular velocity, the ergosphere (static limit), the horizon radius r_+ and the horizon area.

Reader can use the factored equatorial photon potentials V_+ and V_- with a ZAMO's energy condition to decide which trajectories are physical, and explain how negative-energy orbits in the ergoregion allow the Penrose process.
Reader can describe how stellar-mass and supermassive black holes are identified observationally (X-ray binaries, mass gap, stellar orbits at Sgr A*, EHT imaging, gravitational waves).

Reader can reproduce the heuristic derivation of the Hawking photon energy hbar/8M from the uncertainty principle, state T_H = hbar/(8 pi k_B M), derive the M^3 evaporation lifetime scaling, and identify S = kA/(4 hbar) through dM = T_H dS.

teaching_approach.summary: A long chapter that starts from physics and ends in astronomy. Schutz opens with the Newtonian dark star as a foil. He then does orbit theory the way an undergraduate does central-force problems: symmetry gives two conserved quantities, and a squared effective potential turns the motion into a one-dimensional energy diagram, with particles and photons handled side by side. The classic tests are derived perturbatively and immediately converted into numbers for Mercury, the Sun, Jupiter and pulsars. For r = 2M he uses a disciplined 'ask invariant questions' method: an analogy with the pole of spherical coordinates, proper versus coordinate infall time, finite local curvature, the interior signature flip, and then a picture problem (closing light cones) solved by Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates, toured in eight numbered remarks. Kerr is treated only as far as frame dragging, the ergosphere, horizon area and equatorial photon potentials. A recurring idea is that the sign of energy is set by the local forward direction of time, and it links the Penrose process to the heuristic Hawking argument. General theorems are listed rather than proved, and the observational sections are descriptive and heavily referenced.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: can gravity trap light? Michell and Laplace's escape-velocity dark star gives R = 2GM/c^2 and a density that falls as M^-2. Relativity then rejects light rising and falling back, because a local inertial observer would see the photon stop.
Model: time independence and axial symmetry give conserved E and J; normalizing the four-momentum yields a radial energy equation with squared effective potentials for particles and photons.
Qualitative reading: turning points, scattering, stable and unstable circular orbits and plunges are read off labelled potential diagrams; extrema give the ISCO at 6M and the photon orbit at 3M.

First check against Newton: the circular-orbit period is Kepler's law; perturbing about a circular orbit in u = 1/r shows the radial frequency differs from the angular one, so perihelia advance by 6 pi M/r. This is evaluated for Mercury and binary pulsars and linked to S2 at Sgr A*.

Framing: the post-Newtonian regime (weak field, slow motion). Isotropic coordinates reconcile the Schwarzschild far field with the ch8 Newtonian metric, and Newtonian dynamics is shown to be governed by g_00, the curvature of time.

Photons: the orbit equation gives deflection 4M/b (1.74 arcsec at the Sun). The Newtonian half-value is explained by light's speed giving g_rr equal weight, so bending is evidence for curved space. This leads to lensing, dark matter, microlensing and the EHT image.

Puzzle of r = 2M: coordinate singularities in ordinary geometry (sphere poles); finite proper infall time versus divergent coordinate time; finite curvature; inside, r is timelike, so nothing escapes; the Earth-horizon analogy.

Picture: Schwarzschild-coordinate light cones close up, which motivates Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates with 45-degree cones; eight remarks read the diagram (hyperbolae, t = const lines, horizon as a null line, redshift, regions I-IV, collapsing-star caveat).

Generalization: the event horizon is defined globally as a boundary in spacetime; horizon growth during collapse; a later gas infall shows its teleological nature; locally trapped surfaces and Penrose's theorem.
Theorems survey: uniqueness and no-hair, charges, stability, merger settling, area theorem, thermodynamic analogy, singularities, cosmic censorship.

Kerr: metric and Boyer-Lindquist coordinates; g_t phi leads to frame dragging and gravitomagnetism (Lense-Thirring tests); tangential photons at g_tt = 0 give the ergosphere; horizon at Delta = 0 and its area; equatorial photon potentials V_+ and V_-; ZAMO energy condition; negative-energy orbits; Penrose process, Blandford-Znajek jets, ergoregion instability of stars.

Application: real black holes (X-ray binaries and the mass gap, Sgr A* stellar orbits, M87 and merging galaxies, intermediate-mass holes, quasi-normal ringdown, numerical relativity and recoil kicks).

Quantum coda: a vacuum-fluctuation pair near the horizon, where the negative-energy partner becomes real inside because E is a spatial momentum there; the uncertainty principle plus infall time gives E = hbar/8M, compared with Hawking's T_H; M^3 lifetime, primordial holes, Planck mass; rearranging dM gives the first and second laws with S = kA/4 hbar; the information question.
signature_moves: Uses the Newtonian dark star as a foil. It is right about the radius, but the local-inertial-observer argument shows why it is wrong about light trying to leave and falling back.
Handles massive and massless particles in strict parallel (tilde versus untilded E, J, V), so photon results appear as limits of the same machinery.
Puts letters (A, B, C, D, F, G) on points of the effective-potential plots and walks through the orbit type associated with each energy line.
Introduces a deviation-from-circularity variable y, keeps the u^3 term while dropping y^3, and completes the square to show the radial and azimuthal periods differ (k not equal to 1).
Explains the factor of two in light bending with a slow-versus-fast argument: slow bodies feel only g_00, light feels g_00 and g_rr equally, so bending measures spatial curvature.
Tests whether a singularity is real by asking coordinate-independent questions: circumferences at a sphere's pole, proper time to fall in, curvature components in the infaller's frame.
Gives a structured tour of the Kruskal diagram as eight numbered remarks instead of a derivation (the metric transformation is left to an exercise).
Uses a thought experiment in which gas falls in later to make the global, future-dependent nature of the event horizon concrete.

Anchors the idea of negative energy in the local forward direction of time for an observer (a ZAMO outside the horizon, an infalling observer inside), reusing it for both the Penrose process and Hawking radiation.
Replaces the full quantum field theory with a one-page uncertainty-principle estimate, then compares it with the exact black-body result (0.860 agreement).
Turns results into current observational numbers and missions right away (Mercury, PSR B1913+16, J0737-3039, S2, Gaia, EHT, LAGEOS-type satellites, GP-B, GW170817).

sections.title: Trajectories in the Schwarzschild spacetime
sections.summary: The longest section. It opens with the pre-relativistic dark star and why relativity changes the picture. It then derives conserved quantities and effective potentials, classifies orbits, finds the ISCO and photon orbit, and goes on through perihelion precession, post-Newtonian ideas, light deflection and lensing (subsections listed separately below).
key_moves: Escape-velocity balance with v = c reproduces R = 2GM/c^2; mean density scales as M^-2, so very massive dark stars need only low density.
A photon turning around would be at rest for a comoving local inertial observer, which is impossible, so in relativity trapped light cannot even leave the surface.
Stationarity and axial symmetry give conserved E = -p_0 and J = p_phi; spherical symmetry lets the orbit lie in the equatorial plane.
Normalization p.p = -m^2 (or 0) gives (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - V^2 with V^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(1 + J^2/r^2) for particles and (1 - 2M/r)J^2/r^2 for photons.
Differentiating gives d^2r/dtau^2 = -(1/2) dV^2/dr, the analogue of ma = -grad phi, so extrema of V^2 are circular orbits (minimum stable, maximum unstable).
Setting dV^2/dr = 0 gives two circular radii when J^2 > 12M^2, merging at 6M (ISCO); photons have a single unstable orbit at 3M independent of E and J.
An energy line above the potential peak (point F) plunges through r = 2M; for a star of radius R the diagrams apply only for r > R.

sections.title: Perihelion shift: noncircular orbits
sections.summary: Finds E and J of circular orbits and the coordinate-time period, which coincides with Kepler's law. Then perturbs the orbit equation about circularity to show that the orbit closes only after the azimuth advances by 2 pi/k, with k = (1 - 6M^2/J^2)^{1/2}. This gives an advance of 6 pi M/r per orbit, evaluated for Mercury, and notes the much larger shifts for the Hulse-Taylor pulsar and S2.
concepts: orbital period of circular Schwarzschild orbits
key_moves: From the circular-orbit radius formula: J^2 = Mr/(1 - 3M/r) and E^2 = (1 - 2M/r)^2/(1 - 3M/r).
The ratio (dt/dtau)/(dphi/dtau) gives dt/dphi = (r^3/M)^{1/2} and P = 2 pi (r^3/M)^{1/2}, a coordinate time that equals the distant observer's time.
Divide the radial equation by (dphi/dtau)^2 and set u = 1/r; dropping u^3 gives the Newtonian orbit, a harmonic oscillator in y = u - M/J^2 with period 2 pi in phi (an ellipse).
Keeping the u^3 term to second order in y gives a shifted oscillator with frequency k < 1, so the pericenter returns after Delta phi = 2 pi/k.
Expand for J >> M: advance 6 pi M^2/J^2, and with J^2 ~ Mr this is 6 pi M/r = 4.99e-7 rad per orbit for Mercury, or 43 arcsec per century.

sections.title: Binary pulsars and post-Newtonian gravity
sections.summary: Applies the precession estimate to PSR B1913+16 and the double pulsar, explaining how periastron shift plus the combined gravitational/transverse-Doppler redshift and the mass function yield the stellar masses. It then introduces the post-Newtonian expansion, shows that Schwarzschild's far field matches the Newtonian metric of ch8 after a shift to isotropic radius, and argues that Newtonian gravity lives entirely in g_00.
concepts: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time
key_moves: Crude Hulse-Taylor estimate with mean separation 1.2e9 m and M = 1.4 solar masses gives 2.1 degrees per year; a careful two-body, eccentric calculation gives the observed 4.2 degrees per year.
The measured periastron advance is turned around to measure neutron-star masses, combined with the redshift term and mass function.
The pericenter shift is an expansion in M/r ~ v^2: a post-Newtonian correction.
Weak-field Schwarzschild has g_rr = 1 + 2M/r but an undistorted angular part; the substitution r-bar = r - M makes the spatial metric conformally flat, matching Eq. 8.50.
For slow motion dr << dt, so the proper time along a world line is dominated by g_00; Newtonian gravity is therefore equivalent to gravitational redshift.

sections.title: Gravitational deflection of light
sections.summary: Derives the photon orbit equation in terms of the impact parameter b = J/E and integrates it to first order in M/b, finding a total deflection 4M/b. Evaluates it for the Sun (1.74 arcsec) and Jupiter, and notes astrometric satellites (Hipparcos, Gaia) and deflection away from the limb. Recounts the Cavendish-Soldner corpuscular prediction of half this value and explains the factor of two physically.
key_moves: dphi/du = (b^-2 - u^2 + 2Mu^3)^{-1/2}; with M = 0 the solution r sin(phi - phi_0) = b is a straight line.
Substitute y = u(1 - Mu) so the cubic term cancels at first order, leaving dphi/dy = (1 + 2My)/(b^-2 - y^2)^{1/2}.
Integration gives phi = phi_0 + 2M/b + arcsin(by) - 2M(b^-2 - y^2)^{1/2}; closest approach at y = 1/b, reached after pi/2 + 2M/b, so by symmetry the total sweep is pi + 4M/b.
Numbers: 8.45e-6 rad at the solar limb, 6.4e-8 rad at Jupiter's limb.
Factor of two: light moves with |dr| ~ |dt|, so g_rr's deviation from flatness counts as much as g_00's; Newtonian corpuscles feel only g_00.

sections.title: Gravitational lensing
sections.summary: Explains multiple images from rays passing on both sides of a mass and why lensing is universal but usually unnoticed. It then surveys cluster lensing (arcs and multiple images), weak lensing and magnification, dark matter inferred from lens mass models, microlensing and MACHOs, and the Event Horizon Telescope image of M87's black hole, where lensing brings light from behind the hole into view.
key_moves: Two rays from a distant star bent around opposite sides of a lens can cross at an observer, who sees two images separated by about the deflection angle.
Double images are rare for stars because alignment is improbable and extended sources blur them; for clusters the probability and deflections are large enough.
Lens mass models show clusters hold roughly ten times more mass than their stars, distributed smoothly: dark matter, which must be neutral and non-luminous.
Microlensing appears as temporary brightening, not image splitting, as a compact dark object passes in front of a star.
EHT: the ring's inner edge lies within 6M, subtending under 1e-10 rad for M87's hole, which needed Earth-sized radio interferometry.

sections.title: Nature of the surface r = 2M
sections.summary: Asks whether the misbehaviour of the metric at r = 2M is geometric or coordinate-induced. Compares it with the poles of spherical coordinates, computes proper and coordinate times for radial infall, shows curvature is finite there, and demonstrates that inside, r is a time coordinate so everything moves inexorably to r = 0. This makes r = 2M a causal horizon with no local marker.
concepts: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinates inside the horizon
key_moves: On a sphere, theta = 0 is a line on a coordinate map but a single point; invariant measurements (vanishing circumferences) reveal this. In Lorentzian geometry, null separations make such tests subtler.
Radial infall: dtau = -dr/(E^2 - 1 + 2M/r)^{1/2} integrates to a finite value down to and through 2M; for E = 1 the result is (4M/3)[(r/2M)^{3/2}].
Coordinate time dt = E dtau/(1 - 2M/r) diverges logarithmically near r = 2M for every E, because the divergence comes from g^00.
Riemann components in the infalling frame are finite at 2M (Exercise 11.21), so the particle continues inward.
With epsilon = 2M - r, the metric shows g_rr < 0 and g_tt > 0 inside: r is timelike, forcing decreasing r for particles and photons alike, so r = 0 lies in every future.
The Earth-horizon analogy: nothing is locally special at a horizon, but unlike Earth's, this one cannot be recrossed outward.

sections.title: Coordinate systems and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates
sections.summary: Draws radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates, which narrow to vertical at r = 2M, and interprets the infinite-coordinate-time result as a coordinate distortion that stretches a single event into a line. It then introduces Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates, in which radial light rays are always at 45 degrees, and gives eight observations about the Kruskal diagram, including the true horizon, redshift seen from afar, the four regions, and why regions III and IV are irrelevant for a collapsed star.
key_moves: Radial null lines satisfy dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^{-1} (printed without the inverse), so cones close as r -> 2M and world lines reach 2M only at t = infinity.
Guess: the whole line r = 2M in (t, r) might represent less than it seems, as with the pole of a sphere.
Define u, v via cosh/sinh of t/4M with factors (r/2M - 1)^{1/2} e^{r/4M} outside and the swapped form inside; the metric becomes conformally flat in (u, v) with no singularity at 2M.
r(u, v) is implicit, via (r/2M - 1)e^{r/2M} = u^2 - v^2, and keeps its meaning as the areal radius of the symmetry sphere.

Lines of constant r are hyperbolae (timelike outside, spacelike inside); lines of constant t are straight lines through the origin, all collapsing into the origin as in a (t, r) chart; the true horizon is r = 2M, t = +infinity, a null line.
A falling clock emits finitely many ticks before crossing, spread over infinite distant time, which is seen as infinite redshift.
For a star that really collapsed, only the part of the diagram outside the stellar surface's world line applies, so regions III and IV are discarded.

sections.title: General black holes
sections.summary: Generalizes from Schwarzschild to black holes formed dynamically. Defines the event horizon globally, illustrates its growth during collapse and its dependence on the future, introduces locally trapped surfaces and Penrose's theorem, and then lists the main theorems and conjectures: uniqueness, charges, stability and ringdown, the area theorem, thermodynamics, singularities, cosmic censorship. The Kerr material follows (listed separately).
concepts: teleological nature of the event horizon
key_moves: Event horizon defined as the spacetime boundary between events that can and cannot send signals to distant observers in an asymptotically flat spacetime; it is ruled by marginally trapped null rays.
Spherical collapse: outgoing photons from the center are progressively delayed; the last one that just stays at 2M traces the horizon, which grows from zero radius before the star crosses 2M.
Late gas infall example: rays hovering at 2M_0 were actually trapped, and the true horizon was already expanding toward 2M_1 before the gas arrived, so locating a horizon requires the entire future.
Practical substitute: locally trapped surfaces defined on one time slice; Penrose proved they lie inside true horizons, so black-hole formation needs no symmetry.
No-hair: a stationary vacuum hole is fully specified by M and J measured from the far field; the complexity of about 1e60 atoms is erased.
Area theorem (with positive energy density) forbids spontaneous bifurcation of a hole; quantum Hawking emission evades it because quantum energies can be negative.

sections.title: Kerr black hole: metric, frame dragging, ergoregion and horizon
sections.summary: Presents the Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates with a = J/M. Shows how the off-diagonal g_t phi makes zero-angular-momentum particles co-rotate (frame dragging, gravitomagnetism, Lense-Thirring measurements), finds the static limit where g_tt = 0 and counter-rotation becomes impossible, locates the horizon at Delta = 0, and computes its area.
key_moves: Stationary axisymmetric metrics fix t and phi but leave r and theta to choice; Boyer-Lindquist coordinates have the minimum number of nonzero components, with g_t phi unavoidably nonzero.
With p_phi = 0 the raised momentum still has p^phi nonzero because g^{phi t} is nonzero, so dphi/dt = g^{phi t}/g^{tt} = omega: an infalling zero-angular-momentum particle is swept around.

Tangential photons satisfy a quadratic in dphi/dt; where g_tt = 0 one root is zero, so no photon (hence no particle) can counter-rotate or stay static: the static limit r_0 = M + (M^2 - a^2 cos^2 theta)^{1/2}.
Horizon where g_rr blows up (Delta = 0): r_+ = M + (M^2 - a^2)^{1/2}, inside r_0 except at the poles.
The induced metric on t, r = const has a theta-independent determinant factor, giving A = 4 pi (r_+^2 + a^2).

sections.title: Equatorial photon motion in Kerr and the Penrose process
sections.summary: Inverts the t-phi block of the Kerr metric to get omega = -g_t phi/g_phi phi explicitly. It writes the equatorial photon energy equation, which contains an EJ cross term and so must be factored into (E - V_+)(E - V_-), and uses a ZAMO to show that only E > V_+ is forward in time. For counter-rotating photons V_+ dips below zero inside the ergosphere, allowing negative-energy orbits, the Penrose energy-extraction process, Blandford-Znajek jets, and the ergoregion instability of rotating stars.
key_moves: 2x2 block inverse gives g^{tt} = g_phi phi/D and g^{t phi} = -g_t phi/D, hence omega = -g_t phi/g_phi phi = 2Mra/[(r^2 + a^2)^2 - a^2 Delta sin^2 theta], which is positive for a > 0 and falls off as r^-3.
Equatorial p.p = 0 gives (dr/dlambda)^2 proportional to (E - V_+)(E - V_-), with V_+ and V_- meeting at the horizon value omega_+ J and becoming complex for Delta < 0 (no turning points inside).
Direction of time: reversing a geodesic's tangent flips the sign of every observer's measured energy, so forwardness must be judged by a local observer, not by E at infinity.
ZAMO four-velocity (A, 0, 0, omega A) gives measured energy A(E - omega J); positivity requires E > omega J, which selects E > V_+.
For aJ < 0 the curves flip and V_+ becomes negative for r < r_0, so forward-moving photons with E < 0 exist only inside the ergosphere.
A particle decaying inside the ergosphere can send a negative-E, negative-J fragment into the hole and eject a fragment with more energy than the original, spinning the hole down.

In a star with an ergotoroid and no horizon, a trapped negative-energy wave leaks positive energy outward and grows exponentially; in Kerr, the horizon can swallow the wave, and small-a linear stability is proven.

sections.title: Real black holes in astronomy
sections.summary: Argues that uniqueness makes black holes astrophysically simple (with Chandrasekhar's reaction), then surveys evidence: X-ray binaries with 6-20 solar-mass holes distinguished from neutron stars by mass and lack of pulsations, the neutron star-black hole mass gap, Sgr A* weighed by stellar orbits and confined by GRAVITY, M87, galaxy mergers and ejected holes, intermediate-mass holes, quasi-normal ringdown, the history of numerical relativity, and merger recoil kicks.
key_moves: Identifying a compact accretor: steady X-ray pulsations imply a neutron star (a hole cannot carry a misaligned field); an estimated mass above about 5 solar masses implies a hole, since causal equations of state cap neutron stars near 3 solar masses.
Selection effect in the mass diagram: X-ray holes are nearby binaries; LIGO-Virgo holes are distant and must be massive to be detected; isolated objects in the gap would be invisible.
Sgr A*: decades of infrared astrometry plus radial velocities give Keplerian orbits sharing one dark focus and M = 4.15e6 solar masses, confined within roughly ISCO size.
Stationary holes ring down in a few cycles; matching the Kerr quasi-normal spectrum would confirm the final object is Kerr.
Recoil velocity depends only on dimensionless data (mass ratio, spins and their directions), because velocity carries no mass scale.

sections.title: Hawking radiation
sections.summary: Gives a plausibility argument for Hawking radiation. Virtual photon pairs near the horizon can become real if the negative-energy member crosses the horizon before recombining, because inside, the conserved E is a spatial momentum and may have either sign. Matching the infall proper time of a freely falling frame to hbar/2(energy) gives an escaping energy hbar/8M independent of where the pair formed, close to the black-body mean energy for T_H = hbar/(8 pi k M). The section derives lifetime scaling, notes primordial holes and the Planck-mass limit, obtains black-hole first and second laws with S = kA/4 hbar, and raises the information problem.
key_moves: Inside the horizon choose an observer momentarily with U^t = 0, so U^r = -(2M/r - 1)^{1/2}; a radial photon's measured energy is -(2M/r - 1)^{-1/2} p^r, positive for any ingoing photon regardless of the sign of E.
A frame released from rest at 2M + epsilon has E-tilde ~ (epsilon/2M)^{1/2} and reaches the horizon after proper time 2(2M epsilon)^{1/2}.
Equating this to hbar/2(energy) gives local energy (1/4)hbar(2M epsilon)^{-1/2}; redshifting to infinity with g^00 and U_0 gives E = hbar/8M, independent of epsilon.
Exact result: black body with mean photon energy 2.701 kT = 0.860 hbar/8M; the local wavelength exceeds epsilon but is much less than M, so the flat-space treatment is self-consistent.
Luminosity ~ A T^4 ~ M^-2 gives lifetime ~ M^3; 1e12 kg lasts about the age of the Universe; the final second releases about 1e23 J at 1e11 K.
A = 16 pi M^2 gives dM = (hbar/8 pi k M) d(kA/4 hbar), i.e. dE = T_H dS, and the area theorem becomes the second law.

Warns that Hawking's negative-energy partners lie inside the horizon and exist without rotation. Penrose-process orbits sit outside the horizon in an ergoregion. Because the partner is already inside, there is no ergoregion-style runaway, only steady thermal emission.

Closes with open questions: whether weak correlations in the radiation carry information, and the use of Hawking radiation and black-hole entropy as a necessary test for any proposed quantum-gravity method.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Annotated pointers: Schwarzschild's biography, video interviews and conference recordings (Scienceface), history of black holes and Kerr's discovery, tests of GR and lensing texts, separability of Kerr geodesics and wave equations (the Carter constant, Teukolsky), black-hole thermodynamics and quantum fields in curved spacetime, numerical-relativity textbooks and the Einstein Toolkit. Ends with the anecdote that numerical relativity at NCSA helped create the Mosaic web browser.
key_moves: Despite lower symmetry, Kerr geodesics have three constants of motion (energy, angular momentum, and a theta-related constant), and field equations on Kerr separate.
Suggests Parikh and Wilczek (2000) as a sharper version of the fluctuation-near-horizon argument used in §11.5.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations, ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 in geometrized units, with M the total mass and r the areal radius. It describes the exterior of any spherical star and, in full, a non-rotating black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch10 as the starting point. The chapter's stated strategy is to understand its physical meaning by studying its timelike and null geodesics.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.21 computes its Christoffel symbols and Riemann components and shows the curvature invariant diverges only at r = 0.

concepts.name: Newtonian dark star
concepts.definition: An 18th-century idea: a body so compact that the Newtonian escape speed from its surface exceeds c, so corpuscular light cannot reach infinity. The critical radius R = 2GM/c^2 coincides with the Schwarzschild radius, but in this picture light still leaves the surface and falls back.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening motivation. Since trajectories depend only on velocity (weak equivalence principle), trapping light is just an escape-velocity question. The chapter then contrasts it with GR, where trapped light never gets out at all.
concepts.notes: Reused later: Cavendish and Soldner applied the same corpuscular reasoning to predict half the GR light deflection.

concepts.name: escape velocity
concepts.definition: The minimum launch speed at which a projectile's kinetic energy balances its Newtonian gravitational potential energy, so that it just reaches infinity; v_esc = (2GM/R)^{1/2} from radius R.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the Newtonian route to the dark-star radius by setting v_esc = c.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The areal radius r = 2M (2GM/c^2 in SI units) at which the Schwarzschild metric's g_tt vanishes and g_rr diverges. It is about 3 km per solar mass and marks the horizon of a non-rotating black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained first from the Newtonian dark-star calculation, then identified in §11.2 with the horizon of the relativistic solution.

concepts.name: mean density at the Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The Newtonian mean density of a mass M compressed into radius 2GM/c^2, rho = 3c^6/(32 pi G^3 M^2). Because it scales as M^-2, very massive objects become black holes at modest, even sub-water, densities.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to argue that forming supermassive holes needs no exotic physics; Exercise 11.1 checks the 1e9 solar-mass case.

concepts.name: conserved momentum components from metric symmetries
concepts.definition: If the metric components do not depend on a coordinate x^beta, then the covariant component p_beta of a freely moving particle's four-momentum is constant along its geodesic. For Schwarzschild, t-independence conserves p_0 and phi-independence conserves p_phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Eq. 7.29. The chapter stresses that Schwarzschild has so much symmetry that these constants fully determine the orbits.
concepts.notes: In Kerr the same argument still conserves p_t and p_phi, but raising indices mixes them through g^{t phi}.

concepts.name: specific energy
concepts.definition: The conserved quantity E-tilde = -p_0/m for a massive particle (E = -p_0 for a photon). It equals the energy per unit rest mass that an observer at rest at infinity would measure; E-tilde < 1 means bound, E-tilde = 1 means released from rest at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined from the time-independence of the metric so that massive and massless cases can be treated in parallel.
prerequisites: conserved momentum components from metric symmetries

concepts.name: specific angular momentum
aliases: angular momentum per unit rest mass
concepts.definition: The conserved quantity J-tilde = p_phi/m for a massive particle (J = p_phi for a photon), arising from the metric's independence of the azimuthal angle phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced alongside specific energy; with the orbit placed in the equatorial plane it completes the set of constants needed.
prerequisites: conserved momentum components from metric symmetries
concepts.notes: The text on printed p.316 briefly writes L-tilde for the same quantity.

concepts.name: affine parameter for photons
concepts.definition: A parameter lambda along a null geodesic in terms of which the geodesic equation keeps its standard form. Proper time is unavailable for light, so lambda is fixed by setting the photon momentum equal to the tangent, p^alpha = dx^alpha/dlambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated briefly: the photon equation p^r = dr/dlambda is taken as defining lambda.

concepts.name: effective potential
concepts.definition: The function V^2(r) such that the radial motion obeys (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - V^2(r). For Schwarzschild particles V^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(1 + J^2/r^2); for photons V^2 = (1 - 2M/r)J^2/r^2. Motion is allowed only where E^2 >= V^2, and radial acceleration is -(1/2)dV^2/dr.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by solving the four-momentum normalization for the radial velocity after inserting conserved E and J, then plotted with labelled energy lines (Figures 11.1-11.3) to classify orbits.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.12 traces the u^3 (i.e. -2MJ^2/r^3) term, absent in Newtonian theory, and links it to the potential's maximum.

concepts.name: turning point
concepts.definition: A radius where the energy line meets the effective potential, E^2 = V^2, so dr/dtau = 0. Radial motion reverses there while the angular motion continues.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by point G in Figures 11.1 and 11.2: a particle from infinity reaches minimum r there and is pushed back out.
concepts.notes: The text warns that the potential equation governs only the radial part of the motion.

concepts.name: stable and unstable circular orbits
concepts.definition: Constant-r geodesics, possible only where dV^2/dr = 0. At a minimum of V^2 a small radial displacement is pushed back (stable); at a maximum it runs away (unstable). For particles with J^2 > 12M^2 there are two circular radii r = (J^2/2M)[1 +/- (1 - 12M^2/J^2)^{1/2}].
concepts.how_introduced: Read from the extrema A (maximum) and B (minimum) of the potential diagrams, then quantified by differentiating V^2.

concepts.name: innermost stable circular orbit
concepts.definition: The smallest radius, r = 6M in Schwarzschild, at which a massive particle can orbit circularly and stably. It occurs when J^2 = 12M^2, where the stable and unstable circular radii merge at an inflection point of V^2; below it, circular orbits are unstable or absent.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows from the condition for real circular-orbit radii; Figure 11.3 shows the potential flattening to an inflection and then losing its well.
concepts.notes: Emphasized as a property of the geometry, independent of the particle. Reappears in the EHT ring discussion and the GRAVITY confinement of Sgr A*'s mass.

concepts.name: photon sphere
concepts.definition: The radius r = 3M where the photon effective potential has its only maximum, so light can circle the hole on an unstable orbit. Its location is independent of the photon's energy and angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by extremizing the photon V^2, with the remark that E and J change a photon's wavelength but not its path.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name photon sphere; it simply calls it the unstable circular photon orbit.

concepts.name: plunging orbit
concepts.definition: A trajectory whose energy exceeds the maximum of the effective potential, so it has no turning point and crosses r = 2M. For fixed J such orbits are aimed more directly at the hole, with a small impact parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Point F in Figures 11.1-11.2; Exercise 11.11 finds the minimum energy for capture.
concepts.notes: For a star of radius R > 2M, trajectories reaching R simply hit the surface.

concepts.name: orbital period of circular Schwarzschild orbits
concepts.definition: For a circular geodesic at areal radius r the coordinate-time period is P = 2 pi (r^3/M)^{1/2}. It is exactly Kepler's Newtonian formula and equals the period measured by a distant static observer, whose proper time coincides with t.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by dividing dt/dtau by dphi/dtau using the circular-orbit E and J; the coincidence with Newton is noted as accidental.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.8 contrasts this with the orbiting clock's proper time and a static clock's time.

concepts.name: perihelion precession
concepts.definition: The steady rotation of the major axis of a nearly elliptical bound orbit. In Schwarzschild it arises because the radial oscillation frequency is lower than the orbital frequency by k = (1 - 6M^2/J^2)^{1/2}, giving an advance of about 6 pi M^2/J^2 ~ 6 pi M/r radians per orbit in the weak-field limit.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Mercury's 43 arcsec per century residual and relativistic systems (Hulse-Taylor, S2). Derived by rewriting the orbit equation in u = 1/r, perturbing about circularity with y, keeping the relativistic u^3 term, and completing the square.
concepts.notes: Figure 11.4 shows strong-field rosettes with advances of roughly 97 and 130 degrees per orbit. The printed intermediate Eqs. 11.34/11.36 contain a J^2 that should be J^4 (see gaps).

concepts.name: binary pulsar timing
concepts.definition: Using the arrival times of pulses from a pulsar in a binary to measure relativistic orbital effects, such as periastron advance and the combined gravitational-redshift and transverse-Doppler modulation, which together with the Newtonian mass function determine both stellar masses and the orbital inclination.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a far stronger-field arena than Mercury: a crude 6 pi M/r estimate gives 2.1 degrees per year versus 4.2 degrees per year measured.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.18 builds a simplified pulse-arrival-time model around a Schwarzschild mass.

concepts.name: post-Newtonian approximation
concepts.definition: A systematic expansion of general relativity about Newtonian gravity in the small parameters M/r ~ v^2 (weak field, slow motion). First-order corrections include perihelion advance, light deflection and frame dragging; higher orders are needed for accurate inspiral waveforms.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after noting that the step from Eq. 11.37 to 11.38 was a Taylor expansion in M/r, so perihelion shift is the leading correction to Newtonian motion.
concepts.notes: Only the concept is given; no PN field equations are derived.

concepts.name: isotropic coordinates
concepts.definition: Spatial coordinates in which the spatial metric is a scalar multiple of the flat metric, dl^2 = F(r-bar)(dr-bar^2 + r-bar^2 dOmega^2), so no direction is singled out. For weak-field Schwarzschild, r-bar = r - M gives F = 1 + 2M/r-bar to first order.
concepts.how_introduced: Resolves an apparent mismatch between the Schwarzschild far field and the ch8 Newtonian metric; the difference is shown to be a relabelling of the radial coordinate.
concepts.notes: The printed text has a sign slip (see gaps).

concepts.name: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time
concepts.definition: For slowly moving bodies the proper time along a world line is dominated by the g_00 dt^2 term, so Newtonian orbits are determined by g_00 alone. Since g_00 also sets gravitational redshift, Newtonian gravity and redshift carry the same information, and spatial curvature appears only in post-Newtonian corrections.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from dr/dt << 1 at the end of the post-Newtonian discussion, then used to explain the factor of two in light bending.

concepts.name: impact parameter
concepts.definition: For an unbound trajectory, the perpendicular distance between the centre and the straight line the particle would follow in flat space. For photons b = J/E, and photon orbits depend only on b.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined when writing the photon orbit equation; Exercise 11.2 proves the flat-space interpretation.

concepts.name: gravitational deflection of light
concepts.definition: The bending of a light ray passing a mass. For a Schwarzschild mass in the weak-field limit the total deflection is 4M/b (4GM/(c^2 b)), which is 1.74 arcsec for a ray grazing the Sun.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the photon orbit equation with a substitution that removes the cubic term at first order, then integrated in closed form. Historically framed by the 1919 eclipse.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.17 derives the partial deflection seen by an observer at finite distance, (2M/r)(1 - cos)/sin.

concepts.name: Newtonian corpuscular deflection
concepts.definition: The deflection 2M/b predicted by treating light as a Newtonian particle moving at c. It is half the GR value, because it captures only the effect of g_00 and misses the equal contribution from spatial curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical aside (Cavendish 1784, Soldner 1801, Einstein 1908), followed by a physical explanation of the missing factor using the post-Newtonian argument.
prerequisites: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time
concepts.notes: Key message: light bending tests the curvature of space, not just the existence of gravitational attraction on light.

concepts.name: gravitational lensing
concepts.definition: Formation of multiple, distorted or magnified images of a background source by the deflection of its light by an intervening mass. Rays passing on different sides of the lens can reach the same observer from different directions.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the simplest geometry of two rays crossing behind a lens (Figure 11.7), then extended to galaxy clusters with arcs (Figure 11.8).
concepts.notes: The book notes that lensed images in clusters are stretched tangentially and squeezed radially.

concepts.name: weak lensing
concepts.definition: Lensing with small deflection angles that may not split images but does distort and magnify them; the lens can concentrate more light on the telescope than would otherwise arrive, brightening distant sources.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as the regime relevant to cluster lensing at cosmological distances, with magnification singled out as often more useful than image splitting.
concepts.notes: Modern usage reserves 'weak lensing' for statistical shape distortions; the book's usage is broader.

concepts.name: microlensing
concepts.definition: Lensing of a star by a compact foreground object whose image splitting is unresolvable, observed as a temporary, symmetric brightening while the lens moves across the line of sight.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a probe of dark compact objects (MACHOs) of about half a solar mass in the Galactic halo.

concepts.name: dark matter
concepts.definition: Non-luminous, electrically neutral mass inferred gravitationally. Lensing models show galaxy clusters contain roughly ten times more mass than their stars, spread more smoothly than the galaxies; no known particle fits.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises from mass maps of lensing clusters; flagged for ch13.

concepts.name: black hole shadow
concepts.definition: The dark central region surrounded by a bright ring of emission seen in horizon-scale images of a black hole. Lensing bends light from gas behind and around the hole into a complete ring, while the interior region sends little light.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the first 'picture' of a black hole (M87*, Event Horizon Telescope 2019) and an application of lensing; the angular scale is checked against 6M.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the word shadow and does not connect the ring size to the photon orbit quantitatively.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where a coordinate system fails to represent the geometry faithfully (metric components blow up or vanish, or distinct coordinate values label one point) although the geometry itself is smooth. It can be removed by changing coordinates and is diagnosed by coordinate-invariant measurements.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through the poles of spherical coordinates on a sphere (Figure 11.10), where a whole line of the coordinate map is one point, then applied to r = 2M.
concepts.notes: The text stresses that the Lorentzian case is subtler because distinct points can have zero interval.

concepts.name: curvature singularity
concepts.definition: A place where spacetime curvature, and hence tidal force as measured by a freely falling observer, becomes infinite, so it cannot be removed by any coordinate change. More generally, a spacetime is singular where geodesics are incomplete, ending after finite proper time or affine parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the coordinate singularity at 2M: Riemann components in the infaller's frame are finite at 2M but diverge at r = 0 (Exercise 11.21). Later generalized in the list of black-hole theorems.
concepts.notes: The Kretschmann value 48M^2/r^6 is the standard result asked for in Exercise 11.21(d); the book does not print it.

concepts.name: proper time of radial infall
aliases: coordinate time divergence at the horizon
concepts.definition: A freely falling particle reaches and crosses r = 2M after a finite proper time, but the Schwarzschild coordinate time along its path diverges logarithmically as it approaches 2M. The divergence comes from the factor (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} and indicates a failure of the t coordinate.
concepts.how_introduced: First geometrical question posed to r = 2M: integrate dtau and dt along a radial geodesic, with E = 1 worked explicitly.

concepts.name: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinates inside the horizon
concepts.definition: For r < 2M the sign of both g_tt and g_rr flips, so curves of constant t, theta, phi are timelike and r serves as a time coordinate while t is spacelike. Every future-directed timelike or null curve must therefore move to smaller r.
concepts.how_introduced: Seen by rewriting the metric just inside the horizon with epsilon = 2M - r; used to argue inevitable collapse to r = 0 and the impossibility of signalling out.
concepts.notes: Reused in §11.5: inside, the conserved E = -p_t is a spatial momentum and can take either sign.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild horizon
concepts.definition: The null surface r = 2M of a Schwarzschild black hole, separating events from which light can reach distant observers from those it cannot. It is locally unremarkable (finite curvature) but causally one-way.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after showing that nothing inside can send a photon out, with the analogy of Earth's horizon for a ship at sea.
prerequisites: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinates inside the horizon

concepts.name: light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
concepts.definition: In a t-r diagram with Schwarzschild coordinates, radial null lines have slope dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^{-1}, so the cones narrow toward the vertical as r -> 2M. This is a distortion of the chart, not of the geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: First attempt at a picture of the geometry (Figure 11.11); it explains geometrically why infall takes infinite t and motivates finding coordinates with undistorted cones.
concepts.notes: Eq. 11.64 as printed omits the inverse power.

concepts.name: Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (u, v, theta, phi) covering the full Schwarzschild geometry smoothly across r = 2M. Outside, u = (r/2M - 1)^{1/2} e^{r/4M} cosh(t/4M) and v = the same prefactor times sinh(t/4M); inside, cosh and sinh swap and the prefactor becomes (1 - r/2M)^{1/2}. The metric becomes -(32M^3/r)e^{-r/2M}(dv^2 - du^2) + r^2 dOmega^2, so radial light rays are 45-degree lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the 1960 answer to the search for coordinates that do not close the light cones; the transformation is given without derivation (Exercise 11.26 asks for the proof).
concepts.notes: The transformation itself is singular at 2M, which is what allows it to cure the metric's singularity. The book remarks the coordinates are poor far from the hole.

concepts.name: Kruskal diagram
concepts.definition: The (u, v) spacetime diagram of Schwarzschild with angles suppressed. Light cones are at 45 degrees, curves of constant r are hyperbolae u^2 - v^2 = const, curves of constant t are straight lines through the origin, the horizon is the null line u = v, and r = 0 is a spacelike hyperbola bounding region II.
concepts.how_introduced: Figure 11.12 plus eight numbered remarks that read off causal structure, the true horizon, redshift of infalling clocks and the division into regions I-IV.
concepts.notes: The comparison with invariant hyperbolae in SR (§1.7) and with Exercise 5.21 hints at the Rindler analogy without developing it.

concepts.name: infinite redshift at the horizon
concepts.definition: Signals emitted by an object falling toward r = 2M reach a distant observer with ever-increasing delay and redshift. Only finitely many ticks are emitted before the crossing, so the distant observer sees the clock slow and dim toward a stop and never sees the crossing itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Remark five on the Kruskal diagram: an infaller crosses every t = const line up to t = infinity, which reconciles the finite proper time with the observer's infinite wait.
concepts.notes: Also applies to short-wavelength gravitational waves falling in.

concepts.name: horizon as a null surface
concepts.definition: An event horizon is ruled by null geodesics: its generators are the marginal outgoing light rays that neither escape nor fall inward, because the horizon is the boundary between rays that escape and rays that do not.
concepts.how_introduced: Remark six on the Kruskal diagram, then used as a defining property of general horizons in §11.3.

concepts.name: maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime
concepts.definition: The full vacuum Schwarzschild geometry covered by Kruskal coordinates. It contains four regions: our exterior (I), the black-hole interior (II), a second exterior (III) and a past interior (IV). For a black hole formed by stellar collapse, regions III and IV (and parts of I and II) are replaced by the star's interior.
concepts.how_introduced: Remark seven: regions III and IV are labelled but declared beyond scope, with the dashed surface of a collapsing star showing why astrophysicists may ignore them.
concepts.notes: The words white hole and Einstein-Rosen bridge do not appear; MTW Box 33.2G and Chapter 34 are cited.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The property that spacetime approaches Minkowski space far from the sources, which allows 'distant observers', total mass and total angular momentum to be defined from the far field.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as a precondition of the event-horizon definition and of the uniqueness theorem, referring back to §8.4.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: In an asymptotically flat spacetime, the three-dimensional boundary between events that can send a signal (by at least one future light ray) to arbitrarily distant observers and events that cannot. It is a null hypersurface ruled by marginally trapped light rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Abstracted from the one-way property of the Schwarzschild horizon; illustrated by collapse (Figure 11.13) where the horizon grows from zero radius before the star's surface reaches 2M.

concepts.name: teleological nature of the event horizon
concepts.definition: Because the event horizon depends on which light rays escape to infinity eventually, its location at any moment depends on the entire future evolution. For example, a horizon begins expanding before matter that will later fall in has arrived.
concepts.how_introduced: Thought experiment: gas falls into a hole of mass M_0 long after it settles. Rays that seemed to hover at 2M_0 were secretly trapped, and the real horizon had been growing toward 2M_1.
concepts.notes: This is why simulations, which cannot run forever, need a locally defined substitute.

concepts.name: locally trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed two-surface, defined on a single time slice, whose outgoing future light rays are momentarily neither expanding nor contracting in area. Such surfaces can be located without knowing the future and always lie inside (or on) the true event horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the practical tool for numerical relativity after the teleological example; linked to Penrose's 1965 theorem.
concepts.notes: Standard usage distinguishes trapped surfaces (outgoing expansion negative) from marginally trapped surfaces (zero expansion); the book's wording corresponds to the marginal case.

concepts.name: Penrose singularity theorem
concepts.definition: Penrose's 1965 result that, given a trapped surface and reasonable energy and causality conditions, spacetime contains incomplete null geodesics; together with related results it shows trapped surfaces sit inside event horizons and that black-hole formation does not require symmetry.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in connection with trapped surfaces and Penrose's share of the 2020 Nobel Prize.
concepts.notes: The book's summary mixes the theorem's content (singularities) with its consequence for horizons; a tutor should keep them separate.

concepts.name: black hole uniqueness theorem
concepts.definition: Every stationary, asymptotically flat, uncharged vacuum black hole is a Kerr black hole, characterized completely by its mass M and angular momentum J (plus charge Q, and in principle magnetic monopole charge, if electromagnetic fields are allowed).
concepts.how_introduced: Top item in the list of general properties, followed by an extended reflection on how 1e60 particles' history collapses to two numbers and by Chandrasekhar's reaction in §11.4.
concepts.notes: Credited to Hawking (1972), Carter (1973) and Robinson (1975).

concepts.name: charged black holes
aliases: electric charge Q of a black hole
concepts.definition: Black holes that carry electric charge Q (or magnetic monopole charge), measurable by Gauss-law integrals far away. Astrophysical holes are expected to be nearly neutral, so Q is usually set to zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Second item in the general-properties list, together with tidal distortion by surrounding matter or a companion.

concepts.name: black hole stability
aliases: linear stability of Schwarzschild and Kerr
concepts.definition: The expectation, proven for linear perturbations of Schwarzschild (2016) and of slowly rotating Kerr, that a perturbed black hole radiates away all asymmetries in gravitational waves and settles to a Kerr state; nonlinear merger simulations always show rapid settling.
concepts.how_introduced: Items three and four of the general-properties list, supported by Figure 11.14's distorted merging horizons.

concepts.name: Hawking area theorem
concepts.definition: Classically, assuming positive local energy density, the total area of all event horizons never decreases in any process. Consequently, black holes can merge but a hole cannot split in two.
concepts.how_introduced: Item five in the theorems list, related qualitatively to horizon growth during infall; quantified later via the Kerr area formula and turned into the thermodynamic second law in §11.5.
concepts.notes: Exercises 11.29 and 11.37 use it to forbid bifurcation and bound merger energy release. Quantum Hawking emission violates it because it involves negative energy.

concepts.name: black hole thermodynamics
concepts.definition: The correspondence in which a black hole behaves as a thermodynamic body with temperature T_H = hbar/(8 pi k M) and entropy S = kA/(4 hbar) (geometrized units). Changes in mass obey dE = T_H dS, and the area theorem plays the role of the second law.
concepts.how_introduced: Foreshadowed in the theorems list as an analogy between area and entropy, then completed in §11.5 once Hawking radiation supplies a real temperature.

concepts.name: cosmic censorship conjecture
concepts.definition: Penrose's conjecture that singularities visible to distant observers (naked singularities) cannot develop from regular initial data in asymptotically flat spacetimes, so singularities stay hidden behind horizons. It is unproven and, in one form, has counterexamples involving weak null singularities.
concepts.how_introduced: Item eight in the theorems list, motivated by the worry that naked singularities would destroy predictability; the Big Bang is noted as an unavoidable naked singularity.

concepts.name: Kerr metric
concepts.definition: The stationary, axisymmetric vacuum solution describing a rotating black hole of mass M and angular momentum J = aM. In Boyer-Lindquist coordinates its only off-diagonal component is g_t phi, it depends on r and theta through Delta = r^2 - 2Mr + a^2 and rho^2 = r^2 + a^2 cos^2 theta, and it reduces to Schwarzschild when a = 0 (full line element in Eq. 11.71).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without derivation after the uniqueness theorem as the one black hole astrophysics needs; its features are extracted by the same conserved-quantity methods used for Schwarzschild.
concepts.notes: The bibliography notes a hidden third constant of motion (Carter constant) and separability of wave equations.

concepts.name: Boyer-Lindquist coordinates
concepts.definition: The standard (t, r, theta, phi) coordinates for Kerr, in which t and phi are the symmetry coordinates and r, theta are chosen orthogonal to them and to each other, leaving g_t phi as the only off-diagonal metric component. Surfaces of constant t and r are not metric two-spheres, so r is not an areal radius.
concepts.how_introduced: Discussed right after the Kerr line element, with a general argument about how much freedom stationary axisymmetric metrics leave in r and theta.

concepts.name: Kerr parameter
concepts.definition: The ratio a = J/M, which has units of length in geometrized units. A horizon exists only for a <= M; a/M is the dimensionless spin.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined because J has dimensions of length squared; Exercise 11.38 shows the Sun has a/M much greater than 1, so collapse must shed angular momentum.

concepts.name: frame dragging
concepts.definition: The co-rotation imposed by a rotating mass on nearby freely moving matter and inertial frames. In a metric with g_t phi nonzero, a particle with zero angular momentum p_phi still has angular velocity dphi/dt = omega = -g_t phi/g_phi phi, which for Kerr has the sign of a and falls off as r^-3.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by raising the index of a zero-angular-momentum four-momentum: g^{phi t} mixes in p_t. Given explicitly for Kerr after inverting the t-phi block.
prerequisites: conserved momentum components from metric symmetries

concepts.name: gravitomagnetism
concepts.definition: The set of gravitational effects produced by moving or spinning masses, analogous to magnetism produced by moving charges; frame dragging and gyroscope precession are its main manifestations.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented by analogy: Newtonian gravity resembles electrostatics, so spin-dependent corrections resemble magnetism.

concepts.name: Lense-Thirring effect
concepts.definition: Precession of the orbital plane of a satellite, or of a gyroscope, proportional to the angular momentum of the central body, caused by frame dragging. It has been measured for Earth by laser-ranged geodesy satellites and by Gravity Probe B.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the clearest magnetic analogy (spin precession in a magnetic field), with experimental status.
concepts.notes: Strictly, the gyroscope precession measured by GP-B is often called the Schiff or frame-dragging precession, and the orbital-node precession the Lense-Thirring effect; the book groups them.

concepts.name: ergosphere
concepts.definition: The surface where g_tt = 0, which for Kerr is at r_0 = M + (M^2 - a^2 cos^2 theta)^{1/2}. Inside it (the ergoregion) no particle or photon can remain at fixed r, theta, phi or move against the rotation, and conserved energies of some physical orbits can be negative. It lies outside the horizon except at the poles.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by examining photons launched tangentially: at g_tt = 0 one root of dphi/dt is zero, so even light cannot counter-rotate.
concepts.notes: The book uses 'ergosphere' for the bounding surface and 'ergoregion' for the region; usage in the literature varies. Exercise 11.30 proves the static-limit property.

concepts.name: ergoregion
concepts.definition: A region where g_tt > 0, so the time-translation direction is spacelike and all matter is forced to co-rotate. In Kerr it lies between the horizon and the ergosphere; some very compact, rapidly rotating stars could have toroidal ergoregions without any horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalization after the Kerr ergosphere, citing rotating-star models; later shown to host the Penrose process and a stellar instability.
concepts.notes: The name is explained through the Greek root for energy (work).

concepts.name: Kerr horizon
concepts.definition: The event horizon of a Kerr black hole, at r_+ = M + (M^2 - a^2)^{1/2}, where Delta = 0 and g_rr diverges. Radial turning points for equatorial photons disappear inside it.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with Schwarzschild, where g_tt = 0 and g_rr infinite coincide; in Kerr they separate into ergosphere and horizon. Its horizon status is asserted, with only a partial (equatorial) justification.
concepts.notes: The inner horizon r_- is not discussed.

concepts.name: Kerr horizon area
concepts.definition: The proper area of the Kerr event horizon, A = 4 pi (r_+^2 + a^2) = 8 pi M r_+, obtained by integrating the square root of the determinant of the induced two-metric on t, r = const surfaces. It reduces to 16 pi M^2 for Schwarzschild.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed because the area theorem makes area the key dynamical quantity; the integral is simple because the determinant's non-trivial factor is theta-independent.

concepts.name: factored effective potentials
aliases: V_+ and V_- for Kerr equatorial photons
concepts.definition: For equatorial Kerr photon motion the radial equation contains a cross term in EJ, so it is written as (dr/dlambda)^2 proportional to (E - V_+)(E - V_-). Motion is allowed where E > V_+ or E < V_-, and the two curves meet at the horizon at omega_+ J.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed because the Schwarzschild trick E^2 - V^2 fails; plotted in Figures 11.15-11.17 for co-rotating, counter-rotating and stellar cases.

concepts.name: zero-angular-momentum observer
concepts.definition: An accelerated observer at fixed r and theta who has zero angular momentum and therefore circulates at the frame-dragging angular velocity omega; four-velocity U = A(1, 0, 0, omega) with A^2 = g_phi phi/(-D). A ZAMO measures a particle's energy as A(E - omega J).
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as a convenient local clock near a Kerr hole to decide which geodesics run forward in time; compared to a person standing on Earth, held up by their legs.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.40(b) shows a ZAMO measures equal round-trip times for light sent either way around.

concepts.name: negative-energy orbits
concepts.definition: Future-directed geodesics whose conserved energy E = -p_t (energy at infinity) is negative. A geodesic is physical if a local forward-moving observer measures positive energy, which for a ZAMO requires E > omega J. For counter-rotating orbits inside an ergoregion this allows E < 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the observation that reversing a curve's direction flips every measured energy, so the forward direction must be judged locally; then read off from the counter-rotating potentials (Figure 11.16).
concepts.notes: Reused in §11.5 for photons inside the Schwarzschild horizon, where E is spatial.

concepts.name: Penrose process
aliases: energy extraction from a rotating black hole
concepts.definition: A mechanism for extracting rotational energy from a Kerr black hole. A body entering the ergoregion splits so that one fragment follows a negative-energy, negative-angular-momentum orbit into the hole while the other escapes with more energy than the original body. The hole's mass and spin both decrease.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a thought experiment (Penrose 1969) following the discovery of negative-energy orbits in the ergoregion.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.35 proves the angular-momentum decrease. The book states it works for any ergoregion, not only Kerr.

concepts.name: Blandford-Znajek mechanism
aliases: magnetic extraction of black-hole spin energy
concepts.definition: Extraction of a rotating black hole's spin energy through magnetic fields threading the ergoregion and horizon, supplied by an accretion disk; proposed as the power source of relativistic jets in quasars.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a practical realization of the Penrose idea, described via pair creation and negative-energy trapped particles.
concepts.notes: The book's particle-based description is a heuristic; the real mechanism is electromagnetic (force-free magnetosphere).

concepts.name: ergoregion instability
concepts.definition: A runaway in rotating stars that have an ergoregion but no horizon. A negative-energy wave trapped in the ergoregion leaks positive-energy radiation to infinity, which by energy conservation deepens the negative energy, so the wave grows exponentially until the star spins down.
concepts.how_introduced: Heuristic feedback argument after Figure 11.17; contrasted with Kerr, where the horizon absorbs the trapped wave.

concepts.name: X-ray binary
concepts.definition: A binary in which a compact object (neutron star or black hole) accretes gas from a companion star; the gas forms a disk, is heated by friction to over 1e6 K, and emits X-rays. Mass estimates from the companion's orbit identify stellar-mass black holes of about 6-20 solar masses.
concepts.how_introduced: The main route to stellar-mass black holes before gravitational waves, with the criteria (no steady pulsations, mass above about 5 solar masses) for excluding neutron stars.

concepts.name: accretion disk
concepts.definition: A rotating disk of gas around a compact object, formed because infalling gas carries angular momentum. Internal friction (turbulent or magnetic) transports angular momentum outward and lets gas spiral inward, converting gravitational energy into heat and radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Described qualitatively for X-ray binaries; its inner edge near the ISCO underlies EHT and X-ray modelling.

concepts.name: neutron star-black hole mass gap
concepts.definition: The apparent scarcity of compact objects between about 2 and 5 solar masses in electromagnetic samples: neutron stars lie below, X-ray black holes above. The GW170817 remnant falls in the gap, and isolated objects there may simply be invisible.
concepts.how_introduced: Figure 11.18 (masses of known compact objects as of 2018) with discussion of selection effects.

concepts.name: supermassive black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole of roughly 1e6 to 1e10 solar masses found in the centres of nearly all galaxies. SMBHs power quasars and active galaxies and grow partly through galaxy and black-hole mergers.
concepts.how_introduced: Surveyed with Sgr A*, M87, the double-nucleus galaxy NGC 6240, a candidate recoiling hole, and prospects for LISA.

concepts.name: Sagittarius A*
concepts.definition: The supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, about 4.15e6 solar masses and 8.3 kpc away, weighed from the Keplerian orbits of nearby S-stars and confined by GRAVITY interferometry to a region comparable to its ISCO.
concepts.how_introduced: Best-evidence case: decades of infrared astrometry show many elliptical orbits sharing a dark focus (Figure 11.19); star S2 shows relativistic precession.

concepts.name: intermediate-mass black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole in the range of roughly 1e2-1e4 solar masses, between stellar and supermassive holes. Candidates include some bright X-ray sources, globular-cluster centres such as Omega Centauri, and the ~150 solar-mass remnant of a LIGO-Virgo merger.
concepts.how_introduced: Short survey, with possible origins in Population III stars and prospects for LISA.

concepts.name: quasi-normal modes
concepts.definition: Damped characteristic oscillations of a perturbed black hole, radiated as gravitational waves. Their frequencies and damping times depend only on M and a, and they decay within a few cycles, much faster than neutron-star modes.
concepts.how_introduced: In the discussion of dynamical black holes: formation or merger leaves asymmetries that ring down to Kerr, and matching the Kerr spectrum would confirm the remnant's identity.

concepts.name: numerical relativity
concepts.definition: The solution of Einstein's equations by computer, evolving the metric as a dynamical field on a grid. It became able to simulate binary black-hole orbits and mergers stably in 2005-2006 and now supplies waveforms for gravitational-wave searches.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical survey of challenges (horizons crossing grids, coordinate and curvature singularities) and breakthroughs, plus the Mosaic-browser anecdote in the bibliography.

concepts.name: gravitational recoil kick
concepts.definition: The recoil velocity of a merged black hole caused by asymmetric emission of gravitational-wave linear momentum. Because velocity carries no mass scale, it depends only on the mass ratio and the spin magnitudes and orientations; typical values are hundreds of km/s.
concepts.how_introduced: Highlighted as a striking outcome of merger simulations, able to eject holes from clusters or galaxies.
concepts.notes: The book's claim of kicks exceeding 10% of c appears overstated; simulations give maxima of roughly 5000 km/s (about 1.7% of c).

concepts.name: vacuum fluctuations
concepts.definition: In quantum field theory the vacuum continually produces short-lived virtual particle pairs that borrow an energy Delta E for a time of order hbar/(2 Delta E). Energy conservation is violated only on these short timescales.
concepts.how_introduced: The single quantum ingredient of the heuristic Hawking argument, applied near a horizon where spacetime is locally flat.
concepts.notes: A pedagogical picture, not a rigorous description of QFT in curved spacetime.

concepts.name: Hawking radiation
concepts.definition: The quantum emission of thermal radiation by a black hole. Near the horizon, vacuum-fluctuation pairs can separate: a negative-energy partner crosses the horizon, where negative E is an allowed spatial momentum, and a positive-energy quantum escapes. The result is a black-body spectrum at T_H = hbar/(8 pi k M) and a decrease of the hole's mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Plausibility argument: the negative-energy member must reach the horizon within the fluctuation time; equating that time to a freely falling frame's infall proper time gives an escaping energy hbar/8M, which is then compared with Hawking's exact thermal result.
prerequisites: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinates inside the horizon
concepts.notes: The book contrasts it with the Penrose process: Hawking's negative-energy quanta are inside the horizon, not in the ergoregion, so there is no runaway.

concepts.name: Hawking temperature
concepts.definition: The temperature of the thermal radiation from a Schwarzschild black hole, T_H = hbar/(8 pi k_B M) in geometrized units (hbar c^3/(8 pi G M k_B) in SI), about 6e-8 K for one solar mass. It is inversely proportional to mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from Hawking's full calculation after the heuristic estimate; the mean black-body photon energy 2.701 kT is 0.860 times the heuristic hbar/8M.

concepts.name: black hole evaporation
concepts.definition: The gradual loss of a black hole's mass to Hawking radiation. Since luminosity scales as A T^4 ~ M^2 M^-4 = M^-2, dM/dt ~ -M^-2 and the lifetime scales as M^3; smaller holes are hotter and die faster, ending in a burst of gamma rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Scaling argument from the Stefan-Boltzmann law with the horizon as emitting surface, calibrated to 1e12 kg lasting about 1e10 yr.
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.43 asks for a derivation of the calibration and for the mass below which e+e- pairs are emitted copiously.

concepts.name: primordial black holes
concepts.definition: Hypothetical black holes formed in the very early Universe, not from stars, possibly with small masses such as 1e12 kg, so that they would be evaporating today.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to illustrate the observable final-second gamma-ray burst of evaporation; no such events have been seen. Also mentioned as possible MACHOs.

concepts.name: Planck mass
concepts.definition: The mass built from hbar, G and c alone, (hbar c/G)^{1/2} = 2.2e-8 kg, equal to hbar^{1/2} = 1.6e-35 m in geometrized units. It is the scale at which a Hawking quantum's energy is comparable to the hole's mass, so the fixed-background approximation fails and quantum gravity is needed.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the validity limit of all Hawking derivations (E << M).
concepts.notes: Printed with h instead of hbar.

concepts.name: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
concepts.definition: The entropy assigned to a black hole, S = k A/(4 hbar) in geometrized units (k c^3 A/(4 G hbar) in SI), proportional to horizon area. It makes dM = T_H dS hold and turns the area theorem into a second law; its enormous value reflects the information hidden by the horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by rearranging dM = dA/(32 pi M) so that the prefactor is the Hawking temperature; first mentioned in §11.3 as explaining the information loss.

concepts.name: black hole information problem
concepts.definition: The open question of whether, and how, information about matter that formed or fell into a black hole is carried away by Hawking radiation. Perfectly thermal radiation would carry almost none, but subtle correlations might.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised at the end of §11.5 as a question the Hawking effect provokes, with a suggestion that correlations could originate in near-horizon fluctuations affected by the collapsing matter.

concepts.name: Carter constant
aliases: third constant of Kerr geodesic motion
concepts.definition: A conserved quantity for Kerr geodesics associated with theta motion, not following from an obvious symmetry. Together with energy and angular momentum (and the mass) it makes Kerr orbits integrable; wave equations on Kerr likewise separate (Teukolsky).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only in the bibliography, as a surprising feature given Kerr's reduced symmetry.
prerequisites: conserved momentum components from metric symmetries
concepts.notes: Not named in the book.

concepts.name: Painleve-Gullstrand coordinates
concepts.definition: Schwarzschild coordinates using the proper time of observers falling from rest at infinity: T = t - f(r) with df/dr = -(2M/r)^{1/2}/(1 - 2M/r). The metric becomes -(1 - 2M/r)dT^2 + 2(2M/r)^{1/2}dT dr + dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, regular at 2M and with flat spatial slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 11.23, historically the first horizon-regular form (1921-22), with a light-cone sketch showing finite crossing time and a null horizon.

concepts.name: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (v, r, theta, phi) with v = t + r*, where r* is the tortoise coordinate. Ingoing radial light rays are v = const, and the metric -(1 - 2M/r)dv^2 + 2 dv dr + r^2 dOmega^2 is regular across the future horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 11.24, including a T* = v - r diagram to visualize tilted light cones.
concepts.notes: Printed Eq. 11.127 contains a spurious + dr^2 term.

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: The radial coordinate r* defined by dr*/dr = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}, i.e. r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1|, which pushes r = 2M to r* = -infinity and makes radial null lines t +/- r* = const.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Exercise 11.24 as the step toward Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with a remark that it recalls Kruskal's construction.

concepts.name: tidal disruption radius
concepts.definition: The distance from a black hole at which its tidal acceleration across a star (or a body) exceeds the self-gravity or strength holding it together, so it is torn apart. For a star of density rho around a hole of mass M_H it scales as R_T ~ (M_H/rho)^{1/3}, so large holes swallow stars whole.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 11.25 and 11.28 use geodesic deviation to estimate survival near the horizon and the hole mass for which R_T = 100 M_H.
concepts.notes: The scaling is our own summary of what the exercise asks for.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element
